# Get started on the ThreadX Linux simulator

<!-- type: how-to · level: 1 -->

**Needs first:** [Install](../start/install.md)

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED by scripts/gen-board-support.py: starter status -->
> **Status:** Verified on host (merge). From the board support registry: [`nros-board-threadx-linux`](../reference/boards/threadx-linux.md); [Board Support Levels](../reference/board-support-levels.md) explains the words.
<!-- END GENERATED starter status -->

This starter puts a talker on Eclipse ThreadX (formerly Azure RTOS ThreadX)
running as an ordinary program on your Linux machine, and shows its messages
arriving in ROS 2. ThreadX's Linux port runs the kernel's threads inside one
host process, and NetX Duo's BSD socket layer sits on your host's own TCP
stack, so there is no emulator and no network to set up. The build is fast,
which makes this the quickest way to try nano-ros on ThreadX. You write the
talker in Rust or in C; pick a tab and every tab on the page follows.

## What you need

- A Linux host with the [install](../start/install.md) done, so `nros` is on
  your `PATH`.
- ROS 2 Humble with `ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp`. ROS 2 provides the zenoh
  router the talker talks to, and the message definitions the build
  generates the talker's code from.

Nothing else: no board, no cable, no root access. The talker reaches the
router on this machine's loopback interface.

## Provision

```bash probe=30
nros setup threadx-linux --rmw zenoh
```

That fetches the ThreadX and NetX Duo sources, with the Linux port, into a
shared store under `~/.nros`. There is no cross-compiler to fetch: the
simulator builds for your host. It installs no router: the router is ROS's
`rmw_zenohd`.

## Scaffold the project

<!-- tabs -->

### Rust

```bash probe=40
nros new tx_ws --board threadx-linux --template talker --lang rust
cd tx_ws
```

### C

```bash probe=40
nros new tx_ws --board threadx-linux --template talker --lang c
cd tx_ws
```

<!-- /tabs -->

That wrote a workspace with two packages:

```text
tx_ws/
└── src/
    ├── tx_node/                 # the talker: package.xml, Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt, its source
    └── tx_node_bringup/         # package.xml and system.toml: the board, the RMW, the node
```

`tx_node` is the talker, a library with no `main()` that names no board. It
publishes `std_msgs/String` on `/chatter` once a second. `tx_node_bringup`
says what the talker runs on. The ThreadX startup that runs your node is
generated from it when you build, so you do not need to open it for this
starter.

## Run it on this machine

Source ROS 2, then build and run. This first run records the ROS 2 prefix in
the workspace, so later runs of it need no sourced shell (the router still
comes from ROS 2):

```bash probe=50 probe-run=600
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run tx_node --expect 'Publishing:'
```

```text probe-expect=50
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after
```

The talker dials a router on this machine's port 7447, so `nros run` starts
that router, ROS's `rmw_zenohd`, then the talker, and stops both together.
Don't start a router of your own on the same port. The first build compiles
ThreadX, NetX Duo and nano-ros, a minute or two; later builds take seconds.
With `--expect` it stops everything and exits 0 at the first line containing
that text, and exits 1 if the talker stops first.

Without `--expect` it keeps running until you press Ctrl-C. Start it that way
in one terminal:

```bash probe=60 probe-run=120 probe-keep
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run tx_node
```

```text probe-expect=60
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
```

## See it in ROS 2

Leave `nros run` going. In a second terminal:

```bash probe=70 probe-run=90
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort
```

```text probe-expect=70
data: 'Hello World:
```

The talker publishes best-effort, and `ros2 topic echo` defaults to reliable,
which receives nothing from it. That is why the command asks for best-effort.
The router `nros run` started listens where a ROS 2 node on this machine
looks for one, so nothing else needs to be configured.

## If it doesn't work

- **`nros run` stops at once and names the router:** it could not find
  `rmw_zenohd`, or another router already holds port 7447. Source ROS 2 in
  that shell, or stop the other router. To use a router you already run,
  pass `--router <its locator>`.
- **`nros run` stops at once and names `AMENT_PREFIX_PATH`:** this shell has
  not sourced ROS 2, and no earlier build of the workspace recorded it.
- **No `Publishing:` line:** a cold first build takes about 80 seconds before
  the first publish. If it still prints nothing, `nros run` names the
  router's log when it stops.
- **Everything else:** [Troubleshooting - First 10 Minutes](../reference/troubleshooting-index.md).
